devpost_page.title: BlinkAI
devpost_page.tagline: Blink AI gives a voice to those who cannot type or speak. It translates blinks into Morse code, converts them into text, and sends prompts to AI—unlocking seamless, hands-free communication instantly.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: For millions of people living with Parkinson’s, ALS, and other mobility challenges, something as simple as sending a message can feel overwhelming. Most digital assistants rely on voice or typing, but what if those barriers didn’t exist at all? That’s why we created Blink AI—not just another assistant, but an intelligent system powered by a groundbreaking translation algorithm that converts blinks into text, opening a world of possibilities for those who need it most. Because communication should never be limited by physical ability. Everyone deserves a way to express their thoughts, ask questions, and stay connected—and now, they can do it with just a blink.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Blink AI detects intentional blinks, measures their duration and sequence, translates them into Morse code, converts that Morse code into text, and then sends the final text to an AI assistant to generate a response. How It Works: Blink Detection: The Blink AI algorithm tracks intentional blinks, filtering out natural blinking to avoid false inputs. Blink Interpretation: It analyzes the duration and frequency of each blink, translating them into dots and dashes in Morse code. Morse Code Conversion: The Morse code sequence is instantly decoded into readable text, forming a structured message. AI Processing: The translated text is sent to an external AI assistant, which processes it like a standard input and generates a response. Response Delivery: The AI assistant’s response is sent back to the user, enabling a smooth, natural exchange of information. What It Unlocks: Ask Questions & Get Answers – Interact with AI assistants and receive real-time responses. Send Messages with a Blink – Communicate effortlessly without touch or voice. Control Smart Devices – Operate technology hands-free with precise blink commands. Express Thoughts Clearly – A powerful tool for individuals with limited mobility, turning intention into action. Blink AI doesn’t just detect blinks—it translates them into a language AI can understand, creating a seamless bridge between human expression and technology. No voice. No keyboard. Just a blink.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Implementing the Morse Code Algorithm Accurately – Converting blinks into Morse code required precision. The algorithm had to reliably distinguish between short and long blinks, recognize intentional sequences, and filter out involuntary blinks. Fine-tuning timing and detection thresholds was crucial to prevent errors and misinterpretations. Integrating the AI Assistant – Once Morse code was translated into text, we needed to ensure the AI assistant could process the input accurately and return relevant responses. This required optimizing how text was formatted, transmitted, and made compatible with various AI models to provide fast, meaningful, and user-friendly interactions. Balancing Speed and Accuracy– The system needed to be both fast and precise. If it processed blinks too quickly, it risked misreading input; too slowly, and it would feel unresponsive. Achieving the right balance required extensive testing, adjustments, and optimizations.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We developed a fully functional prototype that accurately translates blinks into real-time AI-powered communication. We created one of the first Morse-code-based blink detection systems, turning blinks into a seamless way to interact with AI. We empowered individuals with a new way to communicate, proving that technology can be for everyone.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Technology should work for people—not the other way around. Small improvements make a big difference. Even a 0.1-second boost in response time completely changed the user experience. Good technology isn’t about making things complicated—it’s about making life easier. The best solutions take away barriers, not add them.

sections.heading: What's next for BlinkAI
sections.text: Making Blink Detection Even Smarter – Improving accuracy so it recognizes blinks more naturally, refines Morse code translation, and responds even faster. Helping Blink AI Learn From Users – Fine-tuning the system so it adapts to each person’s unique blinking style, making interactions feel effortless. Expanding AI Compatibility – Ensuring Blink AI works smoothly with different AI assistants and platforms, giving users more choices. Bringing Blink AI to More People – Optimizing it for more devices so anyone who needs it can use it, no matter their setup. Real-World Testing & Feedback – Working directly with users, accessibility experts, and healthcare providers to keep improving Blink AI where it matters most.

sections.text: Payday is Friday. Rent is due Thursday. For millions of people living paycheck to paycheck, that one-day gap is the whole problem: an overdraft fee, a declined card, or the text nobody wants to send: "can you spot me $100?" When we talked through it, two things kept coming up. People avoid looking at their balance until it's too late, and asking for help is the hardest part : it's embarrassing, and it invites questions about your spending. Being asked can be just as hard: the person helping might be stretched too. Banking apps warn you after you're low. We wanted a bank feature that sees the dip coming and quietly arranges help from people who already said yes, without anyone seeing anyone else's money.

How the Network Guardian decides a safe amount. For each supporter, it takes the smallest of three limits, rounded down to the nearest $5: Their cautious lowest balance (5th percentile) over the whole time the money would be out, minus the cushion they keep. The room left in their agreement with this person: their limit minus what's already out. The room left under their total cap across everyone they support. sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Nessie transfers don't carry a recipient , so every move is a transfer on the sender plus a deposit on the receiver. Nessie also truncates cents, so we store integer cents. Never paying twice. A bank call can time out after the money moved. Every transfer is written to a journal before it's sent, tagged, and an unclear result is reconciled against Nessie rather than retried. Postgres advisory locks and compare-and-set updates stop two decisions from racing. Privacy leaks in unexpected places. A "support on hold" notification would have told a supporter when someone was short, and a one-sided offer could have made someone reachable. We ran about 20 security reviews and fixed every finding. Consent without assumptions. Old limits were migrated with no consent; support only becomes active once both people agree. Production surprises: a 5-connection database pool ran out under real traffic, which made the assistant fall back to rules. We raised it to 15 and made it fail fast.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: On June 14th, World Blood Donor Day was observed globally. Many individuals participated, social media engagement increased significantly, and donor turnout was substantial. Five days later, hospitals were still in crisis. Blood supply was down 35% in a month. Some hospitals had less than a two-day reserve. This situation was impactful for our team. The core issue is not a lack of donors or available blood, but rather the challenge of efficiently delivering the correct blood units to the appropriate hospitals in a timely manner — complicated by testing windows, donor eligibility, cold chain requirements, and the need for verified delivery. No patient should be lost due to a lack of coordination among centers that possess the necessary blood units. We developed LifeLink to address these critical moments — enabling hospital staff to request what they need and ensuring the system responds promptly and effectively.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: LifeLink is a multi-agent blood coordination network built on Fetch.ai . Its sole interface is ASI:One — clinicians communicate in natural language, not structured forms. Try it: "Need 5 units B+ whole blood within 72 hours." A network of specialized agents takes over from there: Hospital Agent — receives the request and checks the hospital's own inventory first Discovery Agent — identifies blood centers capable of fulfilling the balance Center Agents — provide real inventory and pricing (American Red Cross, Stanford Blood Center, and Leukolab in our demo) Donor Agents — participate when fresh donations are required, contingent on eligibility Custody Agent — records a hash-chained trail from dispatch to receive Two paths, both real: Normal SLA — planned restock over days; fresh donation when safe, tested stock as backup Emergency QSLA — minutes matter; pre-tested stock only — you cannot use a fresh donation in an ER in 30 minutes Pay only for units that arrive verified. Donors are never paid. Blood always flows donor → licensed center → hospital .

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built LifeLink on Fetch.ai — not as a chatbot wrapper, but as a real multi-agent network that coordinates blood supply end to end. ASI:One + uAgents Chat Protocol — Hospital staff communicate in plain English. The Hospital Agent on ASI:One interprets requests and manages the full workflow — no custom apps, no forms, just conversation. Agentverse — Hospital, Center, and Donor agents are hosted with mailbox registration and Almanac manifests, making them discoverable and reachable from anywhere — not just locally. uAgents with real roles — Discovery, Centers, Donors, Payment, Courier each handle one part of the chain and pass messages to the next. The Orchestrator holds authoritative order state so nothing gets double-allocated. Stripe (test mode) — When a hospital commits to units, we authorize a PaymentIntent per center and hold funds. MongoDB Atlas — Shared state for hospitals, centers, inventory, orders, allocations, payments, and an append-only event log. Falls back to a local JSON store when Atlas is not configured — same code, same flow. *UCP *— Centers expose commerce-style offers and checkout. MCP enrichment — Geo/Maps for real distance and ETA, Notifications for donor booking confirmations.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We turned a real-world crisis into a working agent network in one weekend. A nurse types "Need 5 units B+ within 72 hours" into ASI:One, and LifeLink runs the full chain — stock check, center discovery, tiered quotes, allocation, donor eligibility, Stripe escrow, hash-chained custody, and payment capture only on verified delivery. No fake order IDs. No invented inventory. Every number comes from persisted state and real agent outputs. We built specialized Fetch.ai agents — Hospital, Discovery, Courier, three Center agents, and Donor agents — each with a distinct job, real message schemas, and Agentverse-ready hosting. This is not one chatbot wearing different hats. We integrated the full stack for real — uAgents Chat Protocol on ASI:One, Agentverse mailbox and Almanac manifests, Stripe, AEVs, UCP-style center offers, MongoDB Atlas.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: uAgents aren't just wrappers — they're the product. Agents, each owning one real role, each passing real messages. That is what makes LifeLink a network, not a script. Multi-agent coordination on Fetch.ai is the reason a single nurse's message can trigger discovery, allocation, payment, and custody across multiple centers without anyone managing it manually. ASI:One + Agentverse changes who can use AI. A nurse does not need an app, a login, or training — she just talks. ASI:One routes it to the right agent. Agentverse Almanac makes it discoverable. That is the real impact: AI that reaches people in moments that matter, without friction. Autonomous agents can save lives at scale. Every blood shortage is a coordination failure. With Fetch.ai's multi-agent stack, we showed that you can automate the entire procurement chain — from request to verified delivery — with agents that act, decide, and settle autonomously. That is not a demo trick. That is what this technology is for.

sections.heading: What's next for LifeLink
sections.text: LifeLink is built to grow — from hackathon demo to regional blood network. Regional scale-out — connect real blood banks and hospital systems across the Bay Area and beyond; our multi-tenant architecture already supports multiple hospitals and centers on one orchestrated network Voice-first clinical UX — hands-free ASI:One for nurses in the OR and ER who cannot stop to type Donor experience at scale — mobile onboarding through the Donor Personal Agent, with calendar booking and notifications when a center needs help National shortage visibility — agent-driven dashboards that surface where supply is low before a crisis hits a single hospital Partnership path — designed to align with blood banking associations and hospital procurement workflows, not replace them

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We've all wanted to experience the childhood dream of being an actual wizard, casting flashy and destructive spells at enemies. But existing games that offer anything remotely similar turn that excitement into a series of artificial clicks and button presses, taking away from the chance to feel like an actual wizard casting actual spells. That's why we created Arcane Shell, a first-person PVE game that turns these dreams into a reality by putting a Wii Remote in your hand as a wand and an external tablet in front of you as your grimoire, so every spell you cast and every enemy you defeat makes it feel like you're actually wielding magic and fighting opponents.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Arcane Shell is a first-person PVE game that turns every child's wizard dreams into a reality by bringing the feeling of being a wizard directly into the physical world. Instead of relying on traditional controls, players wield a Wii Remote as a motion-tracked wand. They can aim and cast spells through specific gestures, while an external tablet represents a grimoire, allowing players to create new spells and solve the mini-games required to progress through each stage.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The project was built using Vite and Typescript. We used three.js for 3D rendering for every single prop, map, enemy, spell animation, etc, all procedurally built with code. We also used XInput/WinHID for retrieving Wii Remote input as well as websockets to sync the game functionality with the external screen display used to craft and complete mini-games. Wii remote bluetooth support is not native to Windows, that is, even though Wiimotes have bluetooth, your laptop cannot connect to them without external software. To remedy, we used WiimoteHook to setup a UDP Server so that the frontend can receive what buttons are being pressed. We then used XInput to be able to send haptics to the Wiimote. Impressively, the Wiimote's latency is minimal, as the connection is via bluetooth. We are able to receive gyro, accelerometer, nunchuck and button data at very fast rates, converting gyro + acceleration data into a functional pointer and gestures for the wand-- again a huge shoutout to WiimoteHook. The external display ("book") is much easier, we have a separate dedicated page to the UI for the book, and simply display that page on the tablet. The tablet is a 7" touch screen LCD for Raspberry Pi's, although a Pi is not necessary.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Most AI driving projects end at a function call. We wanted ours to end with a steering wheel turning on its own. Self-driving used to mean hand-built pipelines: one system for lane detection, another for path planning, and another for obstacle avoidance. Deep learning collapsed all of that into one network. In 2016, NVIDIA's PilotNet showed a single convolutional neural net could learn to steer straight from camera pixels. Tesla's modern FSD v12 has since taken the same end-to-end idea onto real roads. One of us is a racing fanatic with a force-feedback sim rig under their desk, and a hackathon is where big ideas get chased. So we asked: could we build that same pixels-to-steering brain in a weekend and have it physically turn a real wheel, one a human can grab back at any moment?

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Model: a CNN based on NVIDIA's PilotNet architecture: 5 convolutional layers that learn road features (edges, lane lines, curves), then fully connected layers that turn them into driving outputs. We added custom late fusion of Forza's live telemetry: the car's speed joins the image features right before the decision layers, because the same corner needs different steering and braking at different speeds. road crop (66×200) ──► 5 conv layers ──► image features ─┐ Forza speed (telemetry) ─────────────────────────────────┴─► FC 100 → 50 → 10 ──► steering, throttle, brake Wheel loop: Forza can only read one controller. HidHide hides the real wheel from Forza, so the game only sees vJoy , a virtual wheel that the neural net can control and also mirror and intake data from the wheel. This allows us to switch between manual driving and FSD without pause, just like on real autonomous vehicles. TMX wheel ──(angle, pedals)──► our runtime ──► vJoy ──► Forza ▲ │ └──── motor turns the wheel ◄──┘ ◄── AI prediction (laptop, over Ethernet) Stack: Python, PyTorch, DXcam, OpenCV, PySDL2, vJoy + HidHide, Forza Data Out telemetry, two PCs over a direct Ethernet link.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Syncing frames with telemetry. Every frame, wheel reading, and telemetry packet is timestamped on one clock. We measured that the screen shows the game 66 ms after telemetry reports it by matching gear changes on screen against gear changes in the telemetry. Hot-lap data doesn't teach recovery. We mostly recorded fast laps, minimizing lap time and chasing apexes. So the model never saw what to do once it drifted off the line, and it couldn't recover after going off the road. It also never learned to use the road markings as guidance but more or less memorized the patterns around each corner. Overfitting. We tuned the driving (steering gain, throttle ramping, and a corner speed limit) and added DAgger : when the AI makes a mistake, we rewind, take over, and drive it properly, and those corrections become new training data. Driving at signs instead of lanes. The network learned a shortcut: steer toward the big "HORIZON" signs rather than follow the lane markings. Crash run-ups in our recordings had taught it that. We cut them from the data automatically. - Lack of Data. We trained all of our dataset during the hackathon, which accumulated up to around 3 hours of driving on one race/map. The model's ability to generalize is poor, but we did try testing it on races it had never seen before, and it was able to steer around some tight corners and perform decently on straights.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: The wheel actually moves. A neural network's steering decision ends up as a real Thrustmaster TMX turning by itself in front of you, driven by a 100 Hz PD loop with static-friction compensation. Getting motor tracking error from 134° down to 9° by throttling commands to the wheel was the moment the whole thing clicked. A real end-to-end pipeline in a weekend: screen capture → telemetry sync → recording → automatic data cleaning → PilotNet-style training → inference over Ethernet → vJoy → Forza → physical wheel → human takeover → DAgger corrections back into training. The human is always in charge. Grab the wheel, tap a pedal, or press a button, and control is yours within a fraction of a second, and every disengagement is logged with its cause. Stale frames, telemetry, or network? The AI backs off on its own. Honest data engineering. We measured the screen running 66 ms behind telemetry by matching gear changes and built automatic crash/rewind/pause detection with adaptive buffers so the model stops learning from our mistakes. A model that beats its baselines on day one. Our first real GPU run cut held-out steering error well below both the always-zero and training-mean baselines, with a live HUD showing the AI's intended path over the game view.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Hot laps don't teach recovery. We recorded fast, clean laps, so the model never saw what to do after drifting off the line. DAgger (rewind, take over, drive it properly, retrain) was the fix, and it reframed the whole project: the dataset is the product. Speed belongs in the model. Late-fusing telemetry into PilotNet made a real difference: the same corner needs different steering and braking at 80 km/h than at 200 km/h. Keep two machines honest. A clean contract between the inference laptop and the game/wheel PC, plus per-failure logging, saved us hours of guessing over an Ethernet cable. In machine learning, the first 99% comes quickly, and the last 1% takes all the work. It was difficult to optimize our inputs and weights through trial and error given the tight time constraints to retrain the model.

devpost_page.tagline: An app that provides a safer route to the places you need to be.

sections.text: PathWise is a walk-home companion for the University of Washington. You pick a destination near campus, and the app offers two walks: the fastest way along the pedestrian network, and a safer one that is willing to take a little longer for streets that are better supported by the city around them. A friend can opt in to follow that walk by text. If you stop, leave the path, or arrive, they hear about it. You keep the map. They keep their phone.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The walk home from campus is a route people already know by feel. Some blocks are bright and busy. Some are quiet, poorly lit, or awkward to cross. A conventional map treats those blocks as the same kind of line. It optimizes for distance and time, then draws the direct walk. That answer is useful when the only question is "how do I get there sooner?" It is a thin answer when the question is "how do I get there comfortably after dark?" We wanted a route that could see the street the way a person does. Streetlights, sidewalks, marked crosswalks, and places that are actually open all change how a block feels. We also wanted the walk to stay a walk. A safer path that wanders across the neighborhood is not a favor. And we wanted someone else to be able to care about the trip without downloading anything. The person walking should be able to choose a friend, and that friend should have already agreed to watch.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The phone app is React Native with Expo. The server is FastAPI. Under both of them is a walking graph for campus and the nearby neighborhoods: the University District, Roosevelt, Wallingford, Fremont, Eastlake, Montlake, Ravenna, and U-Village. OpenStreetMap supplies the pedestrian network. Seattle open data supplies streetlights, sidewalks, and marked crosswalks. Places come from the map, with opening hours attached when we can read them. The fastest route minimizes walking time. We assume a walking speed of 1.35 meters per second. The safer route uses the same streets, then raises the cost of edges that look less supported. For an edge e with walking time t(e) and a safety penalty p(e), the cost is $$ c(e) = t(e)\,(1 + \lambda\, p(e)) $$ The penalty is a weighted average of four signals. Streetlights use weight lights = 0.40, nearby places that are open use places = 0.30, sidewalks use sidewalks = 0.20, and marked crosswalks use crosswalks = 0.10. If $$s_i(e)$$ is how unsupported edge $$e$$ looks on signal $i$, then $$ p(e) = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, s_i(e)}{\sum_i w_i} $$ A dark or empty block costs more, so the search prefers lit, active streets when they exist. $\lambda$ is chosen by search, as high as the path can stand, up to $$\lambda_{\max} = 4$$. The safer walk must also satisfy $$ T_{\text{safer}} \le 1.30\, T_{\text{fastest}} $$ so it may take at most $30\%$ longer than the fastest walk. sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: A safer route is a tradeoff you can write down. "Safer" felt vague until it became a penalty, a set of weights, and a time budget. The $30\%$ cap was as important as the lights. Without it, the search would happily trade a short walk for a long tour of well-lit blocks. We also learned that consent has to be a step in the product, not a sentence in a settings screen. A friend should not start receiving location-tied texts because someone typed their number. Making them send the first message, to a number assigned to their own phone, made the watcher list a list of people who had already raised their hand. The last lesson was about silence in the data. The honest safety score is the one that refuses to invent a dark street where the city simply has no record.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: The graph was the first long fight. Building a walkable network for this part of Seattle, snapping a GPS point to a sidewalk node, and keeping two routes comparable took more care than drawing a polyline. Points that are really the same corner had to be rejected. Streets outside the ingested area had to fail clearly instead of inventing a path. The live walk fought us next. A phone often stops sending new locations when the person stops moving, so a stillness timer never starts unless something keeps reporting the last position. We added a short heartbeat. The opposite problem showed up off the path: a successful reroute snaps you onto a new line so quickly that a "you have been off the route for a while" timer never fills. The route-change text now goes out when the path is recalculated, and the longer off-path text remains the backup when a new route cannot be found. iMessage was the sharpest product constraint. A shared Photon line cannot text someone first, and each person is matched to their own number from the pool. The project page shows one shared number; the assignment list shows the number that actually receives a given friend’s texts. Early on, a friend could text the project number, or our number, and PathWise would never see them. Wiring the watcher list to every assignment, and telling people to text the number on their own row, is what made a second phone show up in the demo. devpost_page.title: Concerto
devpost_page.tagline: what if we made hack the north into a live concert?

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: At concerts, the audience usually participates by watching, singing, or turning on their phone flashlights. We wanted to take that further and turn every audience member’s phone into part of the sound system. Concerto transforms a crowd of phones into a distributed orchestra. Each phone is assigned a musical part based on where its owner is sitting, allowing different sections of the audience to play melody, vocals, or percussion together.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Audience members scan a QR code and open Concerto in their browser. The application automatically connects their phone, synchronizes its clock with the server, and downloads the required audio. To determine where each phone is located, Concerto displays a timed red-and-blue pattern on every participating screen. Cameras record the audience, and our computer vision pipeline decodes each phone’s unique optical ID and estimates its position in the venue. The operator can then: Review a map of the detected phones Select groups using rectangles, a lasso, or adjustable regions Assign Melody, Vocals, or Percussion to each group Control playback from a shared timeline Adjust gain, mute or solo channels, pause, seek, and stop the performance Immediately mute every phone using an emergency control All phones follow the same server-controlled playhead. If optical localization fails, audience members can manually select the left, center, or right section.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Concerto is a browser-based distributed system with four interfaces: The audience experience The operator console A projector view with a QR code and live readiness counts A camera upload interface The frontends use Next.js, React, and TypeScript. A Bun and Hono backend manages device identities, synchronization, assignments, playback state, media uploads, and operator commands. For synchronization, each phone performs NTP-style clock exchanges with the server. We estimate the server-to-device clock offset using the lowest-latency samples. Playback commands are scheduled for a shared future server timestamp instead of being executed when each message arrives. Audio is downloaded and decoded before the show using the Web Audio API. Each phone only plays its assigned channel, but every channel follows the same global timeline. The client also handles browser autoplay restrictions, reconnection, stale commands, audio interruptions, and late joins. Our optical localization worker is written in Python using OpenCV, PyAV, and NumPy. Each phone transmits an 11-bit device ID encoded as an extended Hamming code. The 55-symbol packet includes timing guards, color pilots, a preamble, a run identifier, and two complementary copies of the codeword. The worker tracks screens through the recording, samples their colors, rejects ambiguous observations, and produces a reviewable audience map. Shared Zod schemas validate messages between the TypeScript services and the Python worker. We also u

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The first major challenge was synchronization. Sending a “play now” message is not enough because network latency varies between phones. We had to separate message delivery from execution and schedule every action against a synchronized server clock. Browser audio introduced another layer of complexity. A connected phone may still have a suspended AudioContext , missing assets, or an output path that has not warmed up. We track connection, clock, visibility, audio, and asset readiness separately so the operator does not see false readiness. Optical localization was also difficult. Real recordings include motion blur, occlusion, exposure changes, reflections, compression, and screens that occupy very few pixels. Our decoder therefore treats uncertainty as an erasure, requires bounded error correction, and rejects conflicting or duplicated identities instead of guessing. Finally, the system needed to recover safely. Reconnecting phones must resynchronize before playing, stale commands must not affect a newer session, and disconnected phones must eventually become silent even if they cannot receive an emergency mute message.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Built an end-to-end workflow from QR-code join to synchronized multichannel playback Created a computer vision pipeline that decodes unique phone IDs from recorded screen patterns Designed a conservative optical packet using extended Hamming error correction Built an interactive audience map with click, rectangle, lasso, and region selection Implemented scheduled assignment, playback, seeking, mixing, and emergency mute controls Added resumable, integrity-checked camera uploads Supported automatic reconnect and playback recovery at the current shared playhead Tested the control system with 1,500 simulated WebSocket clients Kept optical, audio, clock, and operator state clearly separated throughout the architecture

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that clock synchronization and audible synchronization are related but different problems. Accurate timestamps help every phone schedule playback consistently, but speaker hardware, browser audio pipelines, and the physical speed of sound still affect what the audience hears. We also learned that computer vision systems should be designed to reject uncertain results. Returning “unknown” is much safer than assigning the wrong musical part to a phone. Most importantly, we learned that readiness is not one boolean. A phone can be connected without being synchronized, synchronized without having audio enabled, or audio-enabled without having the required music downloaded. Treating those states independently made the system much more reliable.

sections.heading: What's next for Concerto
sections.text: Our next step is testing Concerto with a larger group of physical iOS and Android devices in a real venue. We want to measure acoustic timing, camera coverage, network capacity, and optical decoding at different seating distances. We also plan to improve the camera pipeline for smaller and partially blocked screens, simplify the operator workflow, and explore musical arrangements designed specifically for spatial playback across an audience.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Agents that pay people. I saw a YC hackathan where AI agents pay people to do the things the agent can't do itself. That stuck with me, because robotics has the clearest version of that problem: the thing an agent can't do is collect robot data . It can't reset a cube, take over a stuck arm, or record a clean demo. A person with a phone can, and a lot of people will do it for $5. I spent this whole week doing evals. Getting a robot to actually do something is painful. You run the policy, watch it fail, guess why, collect more demos, retrain, run the eval again. Most of my time went to manual steps that could have been automated: setting up runs, resetting the scene, tracking which trial failed and why, converting data, kicking off training, and the small mistakes in between that cost an hour each. Underneath both is cost. Robot data is expensive, and so is the infrastructure to collect, review and train on it. Data companies also aren't set up to collect data for your task on your robot. But someone will give you a few good episodes for five bucks. Scale that out and you have a usable dataset. Robot Deployment is also just hard and tedious, a perfect usecase for agents. So I built GeonosisAI: a factory where agents run the robot deployment loop end to end and buy the exact data the robot needs from people on their phones.

sections.text: No arm overnight. Nobody could be next to the YAM all night, so I built a physics sim of the same arm behind the same adapter and safety layer, and made "sim or real" a fact on every row. Sim and real numbers are never mixed. Droids that have to wait for hours. Agents normally run and finish. I needed them to park on a database condition and resume later with full context, so I built the wait-for protocol and resume bridge myself. Remote inference at control rate. A 157 ms round trip is several control steps. Async action chunks, dropping the stale prefix and crossfading made it smooth. A real arm is not a sim. Gravity pulls joints off their targets, the Jetson's ffmpeg has no H.264 encoder, the arm has to fold back to rest safely after every trial. Each one cost hours.
